questions.text: Given a block can hold either 3 records or 10 key pointers. A database contains n records, then how many blocks do we need to hold the data file and the dense index
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Data file: n/3 blocks
- Dense index (one entry per record): n/10 blocks

Total = [latex]\frac n3+\frac n{10}=\frac{13n}{30}[/latex]

Answer: 13n/30

questions.text:
Consider the following log sequence of two transactions on a bank account, with initial balance 12000, that transfer 2000 to a mortgage payment and then apply a 5% interest.
1.T1 start
2.T1 B old =1200 new =10000
3.T1 M old =0 new =2000
4.T1 commit
5.T2 start
6.T2 B old =10000 new =10500
7.T2 commit
Suppose the database system crashes just before log record 7 is written. When the system is restarted, which one statement is true of the recovery procedure?
questions.solution:
The crash is before T2's commit record, so T2 is uncommitted and must be undone: B goes back to 10000.

T1 committed, so its changes (records 2 and 3) are redone.

Answer: We must undo log record 6 to set B to 10000 and then redo log records 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: We must redo log record 6 to set B to 10500
We must undo log record 6 to set B to 10000 and then redo log records 2  and 3
We need not redo log records 2 and 3 because transaction T1 has committed
We can apply redo and undo operations in arbitrary order because they are idempotent

questions.text:
Consider the following Relationship Entity Diagram(ERP)


Which of the following possible relations will not hold if the above ERD is mapped into a relation model?
questions.solution:
Qualification is an M:N relationship, so it gets its own table (NID, ExamID, QualifiedDate). Exam keeps only its own attributes (ExamID, ExamName).

Putting NID into Exam would only work for 1:N, so Exam(ExamID, NID, ExamName) is wrong.

Answer: Exam (ExamID, NID, ExamName)

questions.text:
Consider the following partial Schedule S involving two transactions T1 and T2. Only the read and the write operations have been shown. The read operation on data item P is denoted by read(P) and the write operation on data item P is denoted by write(P).

Suppose that the transaction T1 fails immediately after time instance 9. Which one of the following statements is correct?
questions.solution:
T2 reads A (time 7) after T1 wrote it (time 2), and T2 commits at time 8 before T1 commits.

When T1 fails, T2 has already committed using a value of A that must be rolled back. Its effects cannot be undone, so S is non-recoverable.

Answer: Schedule S is non-recoverable and cannot ensure transaction atomicity

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: T2 must be aborted and then both T1 and T2 must be re-started to ensure transaction atomicity
Schedule S is non-recoverable and cannot ensure transaction atomicity
Only T2 must be aborted and then re-started to ensure transaction atomicity
Schedule S is recoverable and can ensure atomicity and nothing else needs to be done

questions.text: Consider a B+ tree in which the search key is 12 bytes long, block size is 1024 bytes, record pointer is 10 bytes long and block pointer is 8 bytes long. The maximum number of keys that can be accommodated in each non-leaf node of the tree is ____________.
questions.solution:
A non-leaf node with n block pointers holds n [latex]-[/latex] 1 keys:

[latex]8n+12(n-1)\le1024\Rightarrow20n\le1036\Rightarrow n=51[/latex]

Keys = 51 [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 50

Answer: 50
